body: Identify the solution(s) to the equation given.

DefaultPathway.title: Factor the LHS
DefaultPathway.text: $$x^2+4x+3=\left(x+3\right) \left(x+1\right)$$

DefaultPathway.title: Zero product property
DefaultPathway.text: $$\left(x+3\right) \left(x+1\right)=0$$ if $$x+3=0$$ or $$x+1=0$$

DefaultPathway.title: Conclusion
DefaultPathway.text: $$x+3=0$$ if and only if $$x=-3;$$ $$x+1=0$$ if and only if $$x=-1$$.

DefaultPathway.title: Move all terms to LHS
DefaultPathway.text: $$x\left(x+1\right)=-3\left(x+1\right)$$ \n $$x\left(x+1\right)+3\left(x+1\right)=0$$

DefaultPathway.title: Distributive property
DefaultPathway.text: $$x\left(x+1\right)+3\left(x+1\right)=\left(x+3\right) \left(x+1\right)=0$$

DefaultPathway.title: Zero product property
DefaultPathway.text: $$\left(x+3\right) \left(x+1\right)=0$$ if $$x+3=0$$ or $$x+1=0$$

DefaultPathway.title: Conclusion

title: Horizontal scaling and frequency
body: You are shown two identical-looking sine waves, $$\sin(Ax)$$ and $$\sin(Bx).$$ The only difference is the scaling on the horizontal axis.

steps.stepTitle: The first peak of $$\sin(Ax)$$ occurs at $$x=\frac{\pi}{2}$$. The first peak of $$\sin(Bx)$$ occurs at $$x=1$$. Which graph represents a function with a higher frequency?

DefaultPathway.title: Frequency and period
DefaultPathway.text: The (angular) frequency of a periodic function is $$2\pi$$ over the period: \n $$\frac{2\pi}{P}$$, where $$P$$ is the minimum period.

DefaultPathway.title: Frequency and period
DefaultPathway.text: The larger the frequency corresponds to the smaller period.

DefaultPathway.title: Period and frequency of each graph
DefaultPathway.text: The period of $$\sin(Ax)$$ is $$2\pi$$. The frequency is $$\frac{2\pi}{2\pi}=1$$. \n The period of $$\sin(Bx)$$ is $$4$$. The frequency is $$\frac{2\pi}{4}=\frac{\pi}{2}$$. Note that $$1<\frac{\pi}{2}$$.

steps.stepTitle: What is the coefficient $$B$$ of the function $$\sin(Bx)?$$

DefaultPathway.title: Standard period
DefaultPathway.text: The standard period of $$\sin(y)$$ is $$2\pi$$.

DefaultPathway.title: Compare periods
DefaultPathway.text: The function $$\sin(Bx)$$ undergoes one complete period when $$0<Bx<2\pi$$, or $$0<x<\frac{2\pi}{B}$$.

DefaultPathway.title: Compare period with known period
DefaultPathway.text: The given period is $$4$$. Thus $$\frac{2\pi}{B}=4$$, or $$B=\frac{\pi}{2}$$

title: Phase shift and initial position
body: An engineer is modeling a piston's displacement using $$y=\cos(2x-\frac{\pi}{2}).$$

steps.stepTitle: Find the $$x-$$ value where this transformed wave reaches its first peak. This $$x-$$ value is your phase shift.

DefaultPathway.title: Standard peak
DefaultPathway.text: A standard cosine wave $$\cos(\theta)$$ reaches its first peak when the argument $$\theta=0.$$ In our function, what is the expression that must be zero when the function reaches its first peak?

subHints.title: Finding the location of peak
subHints.text: To find where our new peak is, set that entire argument to zero: $$2x-\frac{\pi}{2}=0$$. Solve for $$x.$$\n

DefaultPathway.title: Solve for $$x.$$
DefaultPathway.text: $$2x-\frac{\pi}{2}=0$$ implies $$x=\frac{\pi}{4}$$

DefaultPathway.title: Right or left?
DefaultPathway.text: Since the peak moved from $$x=0$$ to $$x=\frac{\pi}{4}$$, did the graph shift left or right?\n

subHints.title: Phase shift
subHints.text: The phase shift is $$\frac{\pi}{4}$$ to the right.

DefaultPathway.title: Graph the function
DefaultPathway.text: The dashed line shows $$\cos(2x), $$ a periodic function of period $$\pi.$$ The solid line shows $$\cos(2x-\frac{\pi}{2}), $$ which is the same graph shifted to the right by $$\frac{\pi}{4}$$.\n##figure1.gif##

steps.stepTitle: What is the phase shift of $$\cos(2(x-\frac{\pi}{2}))?$$

DefaultPathway.title: Where is the first peak?
DefaultPathway.text: To find where our new peak is, set that entire argument to zero: $$2\left(x-\frac{\pi}{2}\right)=0$$. Solve for $$x.$$

DefaultPathway.title: Zero product property
DefaultPathway.text: By the zero product property, the argument is zero if $$2=0$$ (not possible) or $$x-\frac{\pi}{2}=0$$, which means $$x=\frac{\pi}{2}$$.

DefaultPathway.title: Phase shift
DefaultPathway.text: The phase shift is $$\frac{\pi}{2}$$ to the right.

DefaultPathway.title: Compare graphs
DefaultPathway.text: Compare the graph of $$\cos(2x-\frac{\pi}{2})$$ in gold and $$\cos\left(2\left(x-\frac{\pi}{2}\right)\right)$$ in blue. \n Both cosine graphs have period $$\pi.$$ The blue graph, $$\cos(2x-\pi/2),$$ has a peak at $$x=\frac{\pi}{4}$$. The yellow graph, $$\cos(2(x-\pi/2)),$$ has a peak at $$x=\frac{\pi}{2}$$.\n##figure2.gif##

title: Tangent and frequency
body: The function $$f(x)=\tan(x)$$ has vertical asymptotes where the input is $$\frac{\pm \pi}{2}$$.

steps.stepTitle: If we transform this to $$g(x)$$ $$=\tan(0.5x), $$ find the new locations of the asymptotes.

DefaultPathway.title: Find new locations
DefaultPathway.text: Find the new locations of the asymptotes by setting $$0.5x=\pi/2$$ and $$0.5x=-\pi/2$$ and solving for $$x.$$

DefaultPathway.title: Solve for $$x$$
DefaultPathway.text:
$$0.5x= rac{\pi}{2}$$ 
 $$ rac{x}{2}= rac{\pi}{2}$$ 
 $$x=\pi$$ 
 Similarly, $$0.5x= rac{\left(-\piight)}{2}$$ 
 $$ rac{x}{2}= rac{\left(-\piight)}{2}$$ 
 $$x=-\pi$$ 
 Compare the two tangent graphs: $$	an(x)$$ has period pi and vertical asymptotes at $$ rac{-\pi}{2}$$ and $$ rac{\pi}{2}$$. $$	an(0.5x)$$ has period $$2\pi$$ with vertical asymptotes at $$\pi$$ and $$-\pi.$$
##figure1.gif##

steps.stepTitle: Does a coefficient $$0<B<1$$ in the function $$h(x)=\tan(Bx)$$ "stretch" or "squeeze" the distance between the asymptotes?
choices: vertical asymptotes are unchanged by this transformation

DefaultPathway.title: Find asymptotes of $$\tan(Bx).$$
DefaultPathway.text: The asymptotes is found by solving $$Bx=\frac{\pm \pi}{2}$$

DefaultPathway.title: Find asymptotes of $$\tan(Bx).$$
DefaultPathway.text: $$Bx=\frac{\pm \pi}{2}$$ gives $$x=\frac{\pm \pi}{2B}$$

DefaultPathway.title: Find the period
DefaultPathway.text: What is the period of $$\tan(Bx)?$$

DefaultPathway.title: Distance between asymptotes
DefaultPathway.text: The period is the distance between the asymptotes.

DefaultPathway.title: Distance between asymptotes
DefaultPathway.text: The distance between asymptotes is \n $$\frac{\pi}{2B}-\frac{\left(-\pi\right)}{2B}=\frac{\pi}{B}$$.

DefaultPathway.title: Understanding the period
DefaultPathway.text: If $$B<1$$, then $$\frac{\pi}{B}>\pi$$, which means that the distance between asymptotes is increasing.

title: Amplitude and Vertical Shift
body: In signal processing, the "Peak-to-Peak" voltage is the total vertical distance from the maximum to the minimum.

steps.stepTitle: Identify the maximum value of the function $$V(t)=5\sin(Bt)+12.$$

DefaultPathway.title: Maximum value
DefaultPathway.text: The maximum value is achieved when $$\sin(Bt)$$ is at its maximum value.

DefaultPathway.title: Maximum value
DefaultPathway.text: The maximum value of $$\sin(Bt)=1$$

DefaultPathway.title: Plug into function
DefaultPathway.text: The maximum value of $$5\sin(Bt)+12$$ is $$5+12=17$$.

steps.stepTitle: Identify the minimum value of the function $$V(t)=5\sin(Bt)+12.$$

DefaultPathway.title: Minimum value
DefaultPathway.text: The minimum value is achieved when $$\sin(Bt)$$ is at its minimum value.

DefaultPathway.title: Minimum value
DefaultPathway.text: The minimum value of $$\sin(Bt)=-1$$

DefaultPathway.title: Plug into function
DefaultPathway.text: The minimum value of $$5\sin(Bt)+12$$ is $$-5+12=7$$.

DefaultPathway.title: Peak-to-peak
DefaultPathway.text: Peak-to-peak voltage is the total span from minimum to maximum voltage.

DefaultPathway.title: Maximum minus minimum
DefaultPathway.text: Take the maximum voltage and subtract the minimum voltage.

DefaultPathway.title: Graphing the function
DefaultPathway.text: The graph of a sinusoid $$5\sin(Bt)+12$$ oscillates about $$y=12$$ between the values $$y=7$$ and $$y=17$$\n##figure1.gif##

steps.stepTitle: Does changing the vertical shift (the +12) affect the amplitude?

DefaultPathway.title: Amplitude definition
DefaultPathway.text: Amplitude is the distance from the midline

DefaultPathway.title: Amplitude and vertical shift
DefaultPathway.text: The amplitude is $$5$$, it is not changed by the vertical shift.

DefaultPathway.text: Apply the law of logarithms for powers. $$\frac{1}{2}\log_2(x)+\frac{1}{2}\log_2(x-3)=\log_2\left(x**{1/2}\right)+\log_2\left((x-3)**{1/2}\right)$$

Recall the law of exponents
DefaultPathway.text: Recall the for products with different bases and the same exponent: $$a**b\cdot c**b=(ac)**b.$$

DefaultPathway.title: Exponentiate both sides with base $$2$$.
DefaultPathway.text: Exponentiate both sides of $$\log_2\left(x(x-3)\right)**{1/2}=1,$$ which gives $$2**{\log_2\left(x(x-3)\right)**{1/2}}=2**1.$$

So the only answer that makes sense for this equation is $$x=4$$.

DefaultPathway.title: Define a new variable.
DefaultPathway.text: Let $$y=\log_{@{n}}\left(x\right)=\log_{x}\left(@{n}\right)$$.

DefaultPathway.title: Rewrite as exponential equations.
DefaultPathway.text: Write the corresponding exponential relationships involving $$y.$$ \n $$y=\log_{@{n}}\left(x\right)$$ implies $${@{n}}^y=x$$ \n $$y=\log_{x}\left(@{n}\right)$$ implies $$x^y=@{n}$$

DefaultPathway.title: Substitute an expression for $$x.$$
DefaultPathway.text: Substitute your expression for $$x$$ into the second equation to obtain the equation: \n $$\left({@{n}}^y\right)^y=@{n}$$

DefaultPathway.title: Apply the laws of exponents to simplify
What must be true about $$y?$$
DefaultPathway.text: Look at $${@{n}}^{y^2}=@{n}={@{n}}^1$$. This equation implies that $$y^2=1$$.

DefaultPathway.title: Solve for $$y.$$
DefaultPathway.text: We have two solutions, $$y=\pm$$ $$1$$.

DefaultPathway.title: Substitute to solve for $$x.$$
DefaultPathway.text: Plugging back into our equation for $$x, $$ we get two solutions. $$x={@{n}}^1=@{n}$$ and $$x={@{n}}^{\left(-1\right)}=\frac{1}{@{n}}$$

DefaultPathway.title: What to do with scary equations
DefaultPathway.text: Look at the equation. It looks scary because there are too many logs! Think to yourself: what operation can I apply to this equation to get rid of one of them?

DefaultPathway.title: Apply cancellation property
DefaultPathway.text: Exponentiation cancels logarithms. \n $$2**{\log_2(\log_2(x))}=\log_2(x)=2**2$$

DefaultPathway.title: Rewrite in terms of exponents
DefaultPathway.text: $$\operatorname{log_2}\left(x\right)=4$$ means $$2^4=x$$

DefaultPathway.text: If $$\theta=\arcsin(x/3),$$ then $$\sin(\theta)=x/3$$

DefaultPathway.title: SOHCAHTOA
DefaultPathway.text: Sine of $$\theta$$ is the ratio of opposite over adjacent for a right triangle with angle $$\theta$$

DefaultPathway.title: Construct a right triangle
DefaultPathway.text: Construct a right triangle with angle $$\theta$$ so that $$\sin(\theta)=x/3.$$ \n Assume a triangle with opposite side length $$x$$ and hypotenuse $$3$$.\n##figure1.gif##

DefaultPathway.title: Find the adjacent side of the right triangle
DefaultPathway.text: Use the pythagorean theorem Adj $$**2$$ + Opp $$**2$$ $$=$$ Hyp $$**2$$ to find the length of the adjacent side.

DefaultPathway.title: SOHCAHTOA
DefaultPathway.text: $$\text{Adjacent}$$ $$=\sqrt{3^2-x^2}=\sqrt{9-x^2}$$. Since $$\cos(\theta)=\text{Adj/Hyp},$$ divide your result by $$3$$.\n##figure2.gif##

title: Identify the rule
body: A diagram illustrating two equivalent arrangements of shapes. The shapes include two squares, three circles, and a lightning bolt. On the left side, the circles and lightning bolt are grouped together, separate from the squares. On the right side, the squares and circles are grouped together, separate from the lightning bolt. An equals sign connects the two sides.

steps.stepTitle: Identify the algebraic rule that is best illustrated by the visual model in the image.

DefaultPathway.title: What do you see?
DefaultPathway.text: The image shows three distinct shapes in different groupings

DefaultPathway.title: Which relationship?
DefaultPathway.text: The groups of images is more additive that multiplicative

DefaultPathway.title: Putting it together
DefaultPathway.text: The image shows three shapes added in different orders, or the associative relationship $$\left(a+b\right)+c=a+\left(b+c\right).$$

title: Identify the rule
body: A diagram shows a grid of objects. There are $$4$$ rows. Each row shows a diagram indicating the sum $$x+1$$, with a block representing the quantity $$x$$ adjacent to a small square block representing the quantity $$1$$.

steps.stepTitle: Identify the algebraic rule that is best illustrated by the visual model in the image.

DefaultPathway.title: What do you see?
DefaultPathway.text: The image shows four groups of the additive group $$x+1$$

DefaultPathway.title: Which relationship?
DefaultPathway.text: The image depicts multiplication with multiple copies of the group $$x+1$$. The image depicts addition, with the block $$x$$ added to the block $$1$$.

DefaultPathway.title: Putting it together
DefaultPathway.text: Putting it together, the image illustrates the fact that $$4$$ copies of $$x+1$$ is $$4x+4$$. This is the distributive rule: $$a(b+c)=ab+ac.$$

title: Identify the rule
body: A diagram illustrating two equivalent arrangements of shapes. The top row shows $$3$$ yellow squares on the left abutting $$5$$ blue squares on the right. The lower row shows $$5$$ blue squares on the left abutting $$3$$ yellow squares on the right. An equals sign indicates that the two rows are equal.

steps.stepTitle: Identify the algebraic rule that is best illustrated by the visual model in the image.

DefaultPathway.title: What do you see?
DefaultPathway.text: Blocks put together represents addition, here we see different combinations of $$3$$ and $$5$$ added.

DefaultPathway.title: Which relationship?
DefaultPathway.text: The relationship is showing that we can add $$3$$ and $$5$$ or $$5$$ and $$3$$ to get the same quantity, in this case $$8$$.

DefaultPathway.title: Putting it together
DefaultPathway.text: The relationship is the commutative rule for addition: $$a+b=b+a$$.

steps.stepTitle: If $$\cos(\theta)<0$$ and $$\sin(\theta)>0,$$ which is a possible value of $$\theta?$$

DefaultPathway.title: Interpret cosine and sine
DefaultPathway.text: The value $$\theta$$ represents a distance (or angle) along the arc length of a unit circle. The $$\cos(\theta)$$ is the $$x-$$ coordinate, and $$\sin(\theta)$$ is the $$y-$$ coordinate, of that point.

DefaultPathway.title: Determine the quadrant
DefaultPathway.text: Since the $$\cos(\theta)<0$$ and $$\sin(\theta)>0,$$ the $$x-$$ coordinate is negative and the $$y-$$ coordinate is positive. This puts $$\theta$$ in the second quadrant.\n##figure1.gif##

DefaultPathway.title: Determine range of values
DefaultPathway.text: Angles in the second quadrant must satisfy $$\frac{\pi}{2}$$ < $$\theta$$ < $$\pi$$

steps.stepTitle: If $$\cos(\theta)<0$$ and $$\sin(\theta)>0,$$ which is a possible value of $$\theta?$$

DefaultPathway.title: Determine range of values
DefaultPathway.text: Angles in the second quadrant have infinitely many possible descriptions. We might have $$\pi/2$$ < $$\theta$$ < $$\pi, $$ or we might have $$\pi/2+2\pi$$ $$k$$ < $$\theta$$ < $$pi+2\pi$$ $$k$$ for $$k$$ some integer value. This is because we could wind any number of times around the circle first before landing at the angle.

DefaultPathway.text: Look at each angle and express in terms of $$2\pi$$ $$k$$ for some $$k.$$

• $$4\pi=$$ $$2(2\pi)$$ lies along the horizontal axis where $$\sin(	heta)=0$$ 
 • $$ rac{5\pi}{2}= rac{\pi}{2}+2\pi$$ lies along the vertical axis where $$\cos(	heta)=0$$ 
 • $$ rac{11\pi}{3}= rac{5\pi+6\pi}{3}= rac{5\pi}{3}+2\pi$$ is in the fourth quadrant. 
 • $$ rac{8\pi}{3}= rac{2\pi}{3}+2\pi$$ lies in the second quadrant

DefaultPathway.text: Recall that $$\cos\left(\frac{-\pi}{6}\right)$$ represents the $$x-$$ coordinate of the point on the unit circle at the angle $$\frac{-\pi}{6}.$$

DefaultPathway.title: Find equivalent angle geometrically
DefaultPathway.text: The principal range of $$\arccos$$ is $$[0, \pi], $$ which covers only the 1st and 2nd quadrants. Angles in the 4th quadrant share the same $$x-$$ coordinate as angles directly above them in the 1st quadrant. Visually, a vertical line drawn up from the point on the circle at angle $$\frac{-\pi}{6}$$ intersects the upper half of the circle at the point on the circle at angle $$\frac{\pi}{6}.$$\n##figure1.gif##

DefaultPathway.title: Find equivalent angle algebraically
DefaultPathway.text: We can also verify this algebraically. Because cosine is an even function, $$\cos\left(\frac{-\pi}{6}\right)=\cos\left(\frac{\pi}{6}\right).$$ Since $$\frac{\pi}{6}$$ falls inside the required principal range of $$[0, \pi], $$ that is our final answer.

title: Bounding trig functions
body: Find the upper and lower bounds of the given trig function.

steps.stepTitle: Upper bound: Find $$k>0$$ such that $$\sin**2(\theta)+5\cos(\theta)\leq{k}$$ for $$\theta.$$

DefaultPathway.title: What is the largest value $$\sin**2(\theta)$$ can attain?

subHints.title: Upper bound for $$\sin(\theta)$$
subHints.text: An upper bound for $$\sin(\theta)$$ is $$1$$, so an upper bound for $$\sin**2(\theta)$$ is $$1^2=1$$.

DefaultPathway.title: What is the largest value $$5\cos(\theta)$$ can attain?

subHints.title: Upper bound for $$\cos(\theta)$$
subHints.text: Since $$\cos(\theta)$$ $$ \leq 1$$, $$5\cos(\theta)$$ $$ \leq 5$$

DefaultPathway.title: Bounding the sum
DefaultPathway.text: By the triangle inequality, we have \n $$\sin**2(\theta)+5\cos**2(\theta)\leq|\sin**2(\theta)|+5|\cos(\theta)|\leq1+5=6$$

steps.stepTitle: Lower bound: Find k such that $$\sin**2(\theta)+5\cos(\theta)\geq{k}$$ for $$\theta.$$

DefaultPathway.title: What is the smallest value of $$\sin**2(\theta)$$ for all $$\theta?$$

subHints.title: Squared function values
subHints.text: A function that is squared is always greater than zero, so the smallest possible value of $$\sin**2(\theta)$$ is $$0$$.

DefaultPathway.title: What is the smallest value $$5\cos(\theta)$$ can take?
What is the maximum value $$3\sin**2(\theta)$$ can attain?

subHints.title: Scaling functions
subHints.text: Since $$\sin**2(\theta)\leq{1},$$ then $$3\sin**2(\theta)\leq{3}$$

DefaultPathway.title: If $$3\sin**2(\theta)$$ is between $$0$$ and $$3$$, what are the possible values of $$3\sin**2(\theta)-7?$$

subHints.title: Subtract $$7$$ from endpoints of range
subHints.text: Subtract $$7$$ from the boundaries: $$0-7=-7$$ and $$3-7=-4$$.

DefaultPathway.title: Find largest in absolute value
DefaultPathway.text: The values range from $$-7$$ to $$-4$$. The largest absolute value (distance from zero) is $$7$$. So, $$k=7.$$

steps.stepTitle: Find a number $$k>0$$ so that $$\frac{10}{2+\cos**2(\theta)}\leq{k}$$ for all $$\theta$$

DefaultPathway.title: Thinking about denominators
DefaultPathway.text: To make a fraction as large as possible, do we want the denominator to be large or small?

subHints.title: Comparing smaller and larger denominators
subHints.text: A smaller denominator creates a larger overall value; for example, $$\frac{1}{2}>\frac{1}{10}$$.

DefaultPathway.title: Find a lower bound

DefaultPathway.title: Bounding $$\cos**2(\theta)$$
DefaultPathway.text: The smallest $$\cos**2(\theta)$$ can be is $$0$$.

steps.stepTitle: Find $$k>0$$ such that $$\left|\frac{(2\cos(\theta))**5}{3**5}\right|\leq$$ $$k, $$ where $$\theta$$ is any number.

DefaultPathway.title: Apply laws of exponents
DefaultPathway.text: Rewrite the expression as a single fraction raised to the power of $$5.$$

DefaultPathway.title: Apply laws of exponents
DefaultPathway.text: $$\left|\frac{(2\cos(\theta))**5}{3**5}\right|=\left|\frac{2\cos(\theta)}{3}\right|**5$$

DefaultPathway.title: Bounding inner expression
DefaultPathway.text: What is the largest value of $$\left|\frac{2\cos(\theta)}{3}\right|?$$

subHints.title: Bounding inner expression
subHints.text: Since $$|\cos(\theta)|$$ $$ \leq 1$$, the largest the inside can be is $$\frac{2(1)}{3}$$ $$=\frac{2}{3}$$.

DefaultPathway.title: Putting it all together
DefaultPathway.text: The upper bound is $$k=(\frac{2}{3})**5$$

steps.stepTitle: Find a number $$k>0$$ so that $$\sqrt{7+2\cos(\theta)}\leq{k}$$ for all values of $$\theta$$

DefaultPathway.title: Inside the square root
DefaultPathway.text: What is the largest value of the expression inside of the square root $$7+2\cos(\theta)?$$

subHints.title: Bounding the cosine

DefaultPathway.title: Include the square root
DefaultPathway.text: If the maximum value inside the root is $$9$$, what is the maximum value of the whole function?

steps.stepTitle: Find a number $$k>0$$ so that $$\left|-3\sin(\theta)-5\right|\leq{k}$$ for all $$\theta$$

DefaultPathway.title: First find the end point values of $$-3\sin(\theta)$$
DefaultPathway.text: $$-3\leq-3\sin(\theta)\leq{3}$$

DefaultPathway.title: Subtract $$5$$ from both end points
DefaultPathway.text: $$-8\leq-3\sin(\theta)-5\leq{-2}$$

DefaultPathway.title: Take absolute value
DefaultPathway.text: Taking the absolute value, we find that the largest possible value is $$|-8|=8$$

DefaultPathway.title: What is the minimum value $$4\cos(\theta)$$ can take?
Put it all together
DefaultPathway.text: The largest possible value is $$12-(-4)=16$$

steps.stepTitle: Find a number $$k>0$$ so that $$\left|\left|5\cos(\theta)\right|-10\right|\leq{k}$$ for all $$\theta$$

DefaultPathway.title: Break into smaller pieces
DefaultPathway.text: First find the range of values of $$\left|5\cos(\theta)\right|$$

DefaultPathway.title: Reduce complexity

DefaultPathway.title: Add another term
DefaultPathway.text: If $$|5\cos(\theta)|$$ is between $$0$$ and $$5$$, find the range of possible values of $$|5\cos(\theta)|-10$$

DefaultPathway.title: Conclusion
DefaultPathway.text: The values inside the outer absolute value are between $$-10$$ and $$-5$$. Take the absolute value, the largest value is $$10$$.

steps.stepTitle: Find a number $$k>0$$ so that $$\frac{20}{7-2\cos(n\theta)}\leq{k}$$ for all values of $$\theta$$

DefaultPathway.title: Consider the quotient
DefaultPathway.text: To make $$\frac{20}{7-2\cos(n\theta)}$$ as large as possible, do we the denominator to be as large as possible or as small as possible?

subHints.title: Subtracting a negative
subHints.text: Since the denominator is always positive, to get the maximum value of the quotient, we want to divide by the smallest value.

DefaultPathway.title: What is the minimum value $$7-2\cos(n\theta)$$ can take?

subHints.title: Find the lower bound
subHints.text: The smallest value is $$7-2=5$$

DefaultPathway.title: Putting it together
DefaultPathway.text: The largest possible value of $$\frac{20}{7-2\cos(n\theta)}$$ occurs when the denominator is $$5$$, which gives $$\frac{20}{5}=4$$

steps.stepTitle: Find a number $$k>0$$ so that $$10\sin(\cos(\theta))\leq{k}$$ for all $$\theta.$$

DefaultPathway.title: Find the largest value of $$\cos(\theta)$$
DefaultPathway.text: $$\cos(\theta)\leq{1}$$

subHints.title: Understanding the range
subHints.text: We know $$\sin(\pi/2)=1,$$ but what about $$\sin(1)?$$ Since $$1<\frac{\pi}{2}$$, we know that it will never achieve the value $$1$$.

DefaultPathway.title: Conclusion
DefaultPathway.text: The maximum value of $$\sin(\cos(\theta))$$ is $$\sin(1), $$ so the maximum value of $$10\sin(\cos(\theta))$$ is $$10\sin(\theta).$$

title: Identifying Equivalence and Lost Solutions
body: When is the student statement true?

steps.stepTitle: A student rewrites $$x^2=9$$ as $$x=3$$. Which statement is correct?

DefaultPathway.title: Losing a solution
DefaultPathway.text: When you take a square root, you have to allow for a negative solution. This step omitted this possibility.

steps.stepTitle: Subtract $$9$$ from both sides and apply the zero product property to find the lost solution.

DefaultPathway.title: Factor
DefaultPathway.text: $$x^2-9=0$$ is the difference of squares, so it can be factored as $$\left(x+3\right) \left(x-3\right)=0$$. This has two solutions, $$x+3=0$$ or $$x-3=0$$. This means we can have $$x=\pm 3$$. The missing solution is $$x=-3$$.

DefaultPathway.title: Factor common term
DefaultPathway.text: $$\left(x+1\right) \left(x+1-1\right)=0$$

DefaultPathway.title: Combine like terms
DefaultPathway.text: $$\left(x+1\right) \left(x+1-1\right)=\left(x+1\right) x=0$$

DefaultPathway.title: Zero product property
DefaultPathway.text: $$\left(x+1\right) x=0$$ if and only if $$x+1=0$$ or $$x=0$$

title: Find all solutions
body: Identify all possible values of $$x.$$

DefaultPathway.title: Cancel the common nonzero factor
DefaultPathway.text: Cancel a factor of $$5$$ from both sides: \n $$5\frac{1}{5} x^2=20\frac{1}{5} x^4$$ \n $$x^2=4x^4$$

DefaultPathway.title: Do not lose solutions
DefaultPathway.text: We cannot cancel the $$x^2$$ because we cannot guarantee that it is nonzero. In fact, we can see that zero is a solution. \n $$4\left(0^4\right)=0^2$$

DefaultPathway.title: Move all terms to the RHS
Factor out the $$x^2$$ from both terms
Recognize the difference of squares
DefaultPathway.text: $$4x^2-1$$ is a difference of squares, so the equation factors further as \n $$0=x^2 \left(2x+1\right) \left(2x-1\right)$$

DefaultPathway.title: Zero product property
DefaultPathway.text: $$0=x^2 \left(2x+1\right) \left(2x-1\right)$$ if and only if $$x^2=0$$ or $$2x+1=0$$ or $$2x-1=0$$

DefaultPathway.title: Solve for the unknown
DefaultPathway.text: The solutions are $$x=0$$ or $$x=\frac{-1}{2}$$ or $$x=\frac{1}{2}$$

title: Problem solving strategy
body: Identify the best first move

steps.stepTitle: In order to solve $$x^4=x^2$$, which is the best first move?

DefaultPathway.title: No division by zero
DefaultPathway.text: Dividing both sides by $$x^2$$ would quietly remove the case $$x=0$$. Since $$x=0$$ satisfies the equation, that step would lose a valid solution and therefore isn’t allowed.

DefaultPathway.title: Square roots lose a sign
DefaultPathway.text: Taking a square root at this stage either loses solutions or forces us to split into several separate cases. Writing $$\pm x^2=\pm x$$ really creates four equations to solve. That’s inefficient and invites mistakes. There’s a cleaner route.

DefaultPathway.title: Why not plug in values?
DefaultPathway.text: While checking values like $$0$$ and $$\pm 1$$ may suggest the solutions here, testing values can never confirm that no other solutions exist. Factoring and applying the zero-product property yields a complete and reliable argument.

DefaultPathway.title: Subtracting $$x^2$$ from both sides
DefaultPathway.text: When we subtract $$x^2$$ from both sides, we can factor an apply the zero product property. Done carefully, this method guarantees that all solutions are found and none are lost.

DefaultPathway.title: Apply step from above
DefaultPathway.text: Subtract $$x^2$$ from both sides: \n $$x^4-x^2=0$$

DefaultPathway.title: Factor out common $$x^2$$ term
DefaultPathway.text: $$x^2 \left(x^2-1\right)=0$$

DefaultPathway.title: Difference of squares
DefaultPathway.text: Continue to factor: $$x^2 \left(x-1\right) \left(x+1\right)=0$$

DefaultPathway.title: Zero product property
DefaultPathway.text: $$x^2 \left(x-1\right) \left(x+1\right)=0$$ if and only if $$x^2=0$$, $$x-1=0$$, or $$x+1=0$$.

title: Solve for $$x$$
body: What is the best first step?

DefaultPathway.title: Cancellation property
DefaultPathway.text: We have a common factor of $$x-1$$ on both sides, but if we cancel it, we will lose the $$x-1=0$$ solution! If you want to start this way, make sure you don't forget to collect the missing solution.

DefaultPathway.title: Expanding both sides
DefaultPathway.text: While you can expand, having that common factor will help us factor in the long run. So don't expand yet!

DefaultPathway.title: Plug in values
DefaultPathway.text: Plugging in values can find you some solutions, but you won't guarantee that you've found them all!

DefaultPathway.title: Move all terms to one side
DefaultPathway.text: If we subtract $$2(x-1)$$ from both sides, we will have all terms on one side, and this allows us to factor and use the zero product property to find all possible solutions.

DefaultPathway.title: Move all terms to LHS
DefaultPathway.text: Apply the first step from the previous part of the problem: \n $$\left(x+3\right) \left(x-1\right)-2\left(x-1\right)=0$$

DefaultPathway.title: Factor out the $$(x-1)$$ term
DefaultPathway.text: $$\left(x+3-2\right) \left(x-1\right)=0$$

DefaultPathway.title: Combine like terms
DefaultPathway.text: $$\left(x+1\right) \left(x-1\right)=0$$

DefaultPathway.title: Zero product property
DefaultPathway.text: $$\left(x+1\right) \left(x-1\right)=0$$ if and only if $$x+1=0$$ or $$x-1=0$$. In other words, if $$x=\pm 1$$.

title: Find all solutions
body: Identify all possible values of $$x.$$

DefaultPathway.title: Cancel the common nonzero factor
DefaultPathway.text: Cancel a factor of $$3$$ from both sides: \n $$3\frac{1}{3} x^3=\frac{1}{3} \left(-3\right) x$$ \n $$x^3=-x$$

DefaultPathway.title: Do not lose solutions
DefaultPathway.text: We cannot cancel an $$x$$ because we cannot guarantee that it is nonzero. In fact, we can see that zero is a solution. \n $$0^3=-0$$

DefaultPathway.title: Move all terms to the LHS
DefaultPathway.text: Rewrite as $$x^3+x=0$$

DefaultPathway.title: Factor the LHS
DefaultPathway.text: $$x^3+x=x\left(x^2+1\right)=0$$

DefaultPathway.title: Zero product property
DefaultPathway.text: $$x\left(x^2+1\right)=0$$ if and only if $$x=0$$ or $$x^2+1=0$$

DefaultPathway.title: Solve for the unknown
DefaultPathway.text: Since $$x^2+1>1$$ for all real numbers, the only solution is $$x=0$$.

DefaultPathway.title: Move all terms to LHS
DefaultPathway.text: Subtract $$2x\left(x+5\right)$$ from both sides: \n $$2x\left(x-3\right)-2x\left(x+5\right)=0$$

DefaultPathway.title: Factor out $$2x$$
DefaultPathway.text: $$2x(\left(x-3\right)-\left(x+5\right))=0$$

DefaultPathway.title: Rules for addition
DefaultPathway.text: $$2x(\left(x-3\right)-\left(x+5\right))=2x(x-3-x-5)$$

DefaultPathway.title: Zero product property
DefaultPathway.text: Since $$2x(-8)=0$$ either $$x^2=0$$ or $$-8=0$$. Since the second is impossible, it must be that $$x^2=0$$ or $$x=0$$ is the only solution.

title: Unit circle
body: Given the number $$\theta$$ find the point on the circle such that the distance traveled along the circumference of the circle is $$|\theta|$$ in the counterclockwise direction measured from the positive horizontal axis if $$\theta>0$$ and in the clockwise direction if $$\theta<0$$

steps.stepTitle: Identify the point on the unit circle corresponding to $$\theta=\frac{\pi}{4}.$$ \n Note that the point A is $$\frac{1}{8}$$ around the circle in the counterclockwise direction measured from the positive horizontal axis; B is $$\frac{1}{4}$$ C is $$\frac{5}{8}$$ D is $$\frac{7}{8}$$.

DefaultPathway.title: Circumference
DefaultPathway.text: The circumference of a unit circle is $$2\pi$$.

DefaultPathway.title: Fraction of the circumference
DefaultPathway.text: If $$\theta=\pi/4$$ then the total circumference of the circle travelled is $$\frac{\frac{\pi}{4}}{2\pi}$$

DefaultPathway.title: Identify the point

title: Estimate the logarithm.
body: Find the largest integer $$A$$ and the smallest integer $$B$$ so that $$A<\log_{3}\left(21\right)<B$$.
lesson: A2.1.3 Log and Exp are Inverses

steps.stepBody: Find the largest integer $$A$$ so that $$A<\log_{3}\left(21\right)$$.

DefaultPathway.title: A simpler question
DefaultPathway.text: What is $$3^2$$?

DefaultPathway.title: Relate to original problem
DefaultPathway.text: Observe that $$3^2=9<21$$. So $$\log_{3}\left(9\right)<\log_{3}\left(21\right)$$ (because logs are increasing functions).

DefaultPathway.title: Simplified further
DefaultPathway.text: Evaluate $$\log_{3}\left(9\right)=\log_{3}\left(3^2\right)$$.

subHints.title: Definition of logarithm
subHints.text: Recall that $$\log_{3}\left(3^2\right)$$ is asking for the power c so that $$3^c=3^2$$

DefaultPathway.title: Is there another integer power of $$3$$ between $$9$$ and 21?

steps.stepBody: Find the smallest integer $$B$$ so that $$\log_{3}\left(21\right)<B$$.

DefaultPathway.title: A related question
DefaultPathway.text: What is $$3^3$$?

DefaultPathway.title: Relate to original problem
DefaultPathway.text: Observe that $$21<3^3=27$$. So $$\log_{3}\left(21\right)<\log_{3}\left(27\right)$$ (because logs are increasing functions).

DefaultPathway.title: A related question
DefaultPathway.text: What is $$\log_{3}\left(27\right)$$?

subHints.title: Simplified further
subHints.text: $$\log_{3}\left(27\right)=\log_{3}\left(3^3\right)=3$$

DefaultPathway.title: Conclusion
DefaultPathway.text: Since $$9<21<27$$, it follows that $$2<\log_{3}\left(21\right)<3$$.

title: Restricted domains
body: Identify the restricted domain on which $$\sin(x)$$ has an inverse.

steps.stepTitle: To define an inverse for $$\sin(x), $$ we must choose an interval where the function is strictly monotonic. Which of the following is a valid (though non-standard) restricted domain for $$\sin(x)$$ that would allow for an inverse?

DefaultPathway.title: Increasing or decreasing
DefaultPathway.text: Look for an interval where the function is either strictly increasing or strictly decreasing. If it does both, it fails the Horizontal Line Test.

DefaultPathway.title: Test midpoints and end points
DefaultPathway.text: Test the midpoints and endpoints. For example, in $$[0, \pi], $$ $$\sin(\pi/4)\approx$$ $$0.707$$ and $$\sin(3\pi/4)\approx$$ $$0.707$$. Since two different inputs give the same output, it is not $$1-1$$.

DefaultPathway.title: Graph the function
DefaultPathway.text: Visualize the sine wave. Between $$x=\pi/2$$ (a peak) and $$x=3\pi/2$$ (a valley), the function is strictly decreasing. This makes it a valid candidate for an inverse.\n##figure1.gif##

title: Identifying Equivalent Fractions
body: Find the equivalent fraction

DefaultPathway.title: Equivalent fractions
DefaultPathway.text:
Two fractions are equivalent if we can recognize one of two relationships: 
 - $$ rac{a}{b}= rac{c}{d}$$ and $$ad=bc$$ 
 - $$ rac{b}{c}= rac{ab}{ac}$$ if a
eq $$0$$.

DefaultPathway.title: Example $$1$$
DefaultPathway.text: $$x+\frac{1}{x}$$ is not equivalent to $$\frac{x+1}{x}$$. One way to see this is to plug in values. When $$x=2$$, $$x+\frac{1}{x}$$ is $$2.5$$, but $$\frac{x+1}{x}=1.5$$.

DefaultPathway.title: Example $$2$$
DefaultPathway.text: $$1-x$$ is not equivalent to $$\frac{x+1}{x}$$. One way to see this is to plug in values. When $$x=1$$, $$1-x=0$$, but $$\frac{x+1}{x}=2$$.

DefaultPathway.title: Example $$3$$
DefaultPathway.text: $$\frac{x^2-1}{x^2-x}$$ is not equivalent to $$\frac{x+1}{x}$$. Note that $$\frac{x^2-1}{x^2-x}=\frac{\left(x-1\right) \left(x+1\right)}{\left(x-1\right) x}$$. While this is of the form $$\frac{ab}{ac}$$, the issue here is that the multiple $$x-1$$ is not necessarily nonzero. So this expression is equivalent to $$\frac{x+1}{x}$$ only when $$x-1$$ is not zero.

DefaultPathway.title: Example $$4$$
DefaultPathway.text: $$\frac{2\left(x+1\right)}{2x}$$ is equivalent to $$\frac{x+1}{x}$$ since the numerator and denominator are both multiplied by the nonzero constant $$2$$.

DefaultPathway.title: Multiply by $$\frac{x}{x}$$
DefaultPathway.text: To see that the two expressions are equivalent for most values of $$x$$, we multiply the right-hand side by $$\frac{x}{x}$$. This gives $$\frac{x}{x+\frac{x}{x}}=\frac{x}{x+1}$$, which is equal to the left-hand side.

DefaultPathway.title: Interpret equivalence
DefaultPathway.text: We multiplied the left-hand side by $$\frac{x}{x}$$, which is undefined when $$x=0$$, so this forces the equivalence to fail at least when $$x=0$$. So whenever both the LHS and RHS are defined, they are equivalent.

subHints.title: LHS
subHints.text: $$\frac{x}{x+1}$$ is undefined when the denominator is zero: $$x+1=0$$. That is, it is undefined when $$x=-1$$.

DefaultPathway.title: RHS
DefaultPathway.text: For which values of $$x$$ is the right-hand side $$\frac{1}{1+\frac{1}{x}}$$ undefined?

subHints.title: RHS
subHints.text: $$\frac{1}{1+\frac{1}{x}}$$ is undefined when $$\frac{1}{x}$$ is undefined and when $$1+\frac{1}{x}=0$$. This happens when $$x=0$$ or when $$x=-1$$.

DefaultPathway.title: Conclusion
DefaultPathway.text:
An equation cannot be true at any value where either side is undefined. 
 - The left hand side is undefined for $$x=-1$$ 
 - The right hand side is undefined when $$x=0$$ and $$x=-1$$. 
 
 Ruling out every value that causes a problem on either side, we see that the equivalence fails when $$x=0$$ and $$x=-1$$.

title: Determine if the expression is true or false
body: Apply general rules to show it is true, or find a counterexample to show it is false.

DefaultPathway.title: Plug in numbers to see if it holds
DefaultPathway.text: If it is false, it won't hold for some numbers. We can try to search for a counter example. In this case, if we take $$a=1$$ and $$b=2$$, we get $$2\left(1+2\right)=2+4=6$$ which is true. Trying other easy numbers, we find all the examples are true. So maybe it is true.

DefaultPathway.title: Relate to another rule
DefaultPathway.text: This looks like the distributive property but from the left side. Let's apply known rules to see if we can generate this new rule.

DefaultPathway.title: Apply commutativity
DefaultPathway.text: $$\left(a+b\right) b=b\left(a+b\right)$$

DefaultPathway.title: Apply distributivity
DefaultPathway.text: $$b\left(a+b\right)=ba+b^2$$

DefaultPathway.title: Conclusion
DefaultPathway.text: Applying known algebraic properties, we were able to deduce that this statement is true.

DefaultPathway.text: Let $$a=1$$ and $$b=1$$, then the left hand side is $$\left(1+1\right)^2=4$$, but the right hand side is $$1^2+1^2=2$$. Since this expression doesn't hold for these specific numbers, it must be false.

title: How to show general property is true

stepAnswer: Rearrange the equation using known rules.

DefaultPathway.title: Ask AI
DefaultPathway.text: As of yet, this does not constitute proof! AI can hallucinate or lie to you. \n A proof is a logically airtight reason that something is true.

DefaultPathway.title: Plug into a calculator
DefaultPathway.text: This isn't really a proof. You can't offload the thinking to a machine.

DefaultPathway.title: Plug in several numbers
DefaultPathway.text: If you can show that the general expression is true for many specific cases, this is gathering evidence that the general equation may be true. However, it is not a proof. You cannot plug in ever single case, which would be necessary with this plug in approach.

DefaultPathway.title: Apply what is known
DefaultPathway.text: Yes, if you can apply a sequence of known true rearrangements of an algebraic expression to obtain the other side of an equation, and you can verify each step carefully along the way, you have shown that it is a true general equation.

title: Algebra of fractions
body: Write the given as a single, simplified fraction expression $$\frac{a}{b}$$.

steps.stepTitle: Give $$h\neq$$ $$0, $$ write $$\frac{\frac{1}{x+h}-\frac{1}{x}}{h}=\frac{a}{b}$$ as a single, simplified fraction, cancelling all nonzero terms common to numerator and denominator. \n What is the denominator $$b?$$ (Let all negative signs be carried on the numerator.)

DefaultPathway.title: Find a common denominator
DefaultPathway.text: To perform the operation $$\frac{1}{x+h}-\frac{1}{x}$$, we find a common denominator. That common denominator is the product of the two denominators $$x\left(x+h\right)$$.

DefaultPathway.title: Find a common denominator
DefaultPathway.text: To create an expression with common denominators, we multiply the first term by $$\frac{x}{x}$$ and the second term by $$\frac{x+h}{x+h}$$. \n $$\frac{1}{x+h} \frac{x}{x}-\frac{1}{x} \frac{x+h}{x+h}=\frac{x}{x\left(x+h\right)}-\frac{x+h}{x\left(x+h\right)}$$

DefaultPathway.title: Add numerators
DefaultPathway.text: Apply the rule for adding or subracting fraction with a common denominator: \n $$\frac{a}{c}\pm \frac{b}{c}=\frac{a\pm b}{c}$$.

DefaultPathway.title: Add numerators
DefaultPathway.text: $$\frac{x}{x\left(x+h\right)}-\frac{x+h}{x\left(x+h\right)}=$$ $$\frac{x-(x+h)}{x(x+h)}$$ $$=\frac{\left(-h\right)}{x\left(x+h\right)}$$

DefaultPathway.title: Turn denominator into a fraction
DefaultPathway.text: Write $$\frac{\frac{1}{x+h}-\frac{1}{x}}{h}=\frac{\frac{-h}{x(x+h)}}{h}=\frac{\frac{-h}{x(x+h)}}{\frac{h}{1}}.$$ Here, we used the fact tha $$h=\frac{h}{1}$$.

DefaultPathway.title: Divide fractions
DefaultPathway.text: To divide by a fraction, we multiply by the reciprocal.

DefaultPathway.title: Divide fractions
DefaultPathway.text: $$\frac{\frac{-h}{x(x+h)}}{\frac{h}{1}}=\frac{-h}{x(x+h)}\left(\frac1{h}\right)=\frac{-1}{x(x+h)}$$

steps.stepTitle: What is the numerator $$a$$ when you write $$\frac{\frac{1}{x+h}-\frac{1}{x}}{h}=\frac{a}{b}$$ as a single, simplified fraction $$\frac{a}{b}$$ with common, nonzero terms in numerator and denominator canceled?

DefaultPathway.title: Apply part a
DefaultPathway.text: We saw that $$\frac{\frac{1}{x+h}-\frac{1}{x}}{h}=\frac{-1}{x(x+h)}.$$ The numerator is $$-1$$.

DefaultPathway.title: Hidden quadratic
DefaultPathway.text: This equation looks like a quadratic equation $${au}^2+bu+c=0$$, where $$u=\frac{x}{x+1}$$. Rewrite the left-hand side of the equation in terms of $$u.$$

subHints.title: Substitute u
subHints.text: Substitute u for $$\frac{x}{x+1}$$ everywhere to get $$u^2+4u-5=0$$

DefaultPathway.title: Factor equation
DefaultPathway.text: $$u^2+4u-5=\left(u+5\right) \left(u-1\right)$$

DefaultPathway.title: Zero product property
DefaultPathway.text: $$\left(u+5\right) \left(u-1\right)=0$$ if and only if $$u+5=0$$ or $$u-1=0$$

DefaultPathway.title: Substitute $$x$$
DefaultPathway.text: Replace u with $$\frac{x}{x+1}$$ and solve for $$x$$.

DefaultPathway.title: Substitute
DefaultPathway.text: $$u+5=0$$ becomes $$\frac{x}{x+1}+5=0$$, which is true if and only if $$x+5\left(x+1\right)=0$$ or $$x=\frac{-5}{6}$$. \n $$u-1=0$$ becomes $$\frac{x}{x+1}-1=0$$ if and only if $$x-x+1=0$$ or $$-1=0$$, which doesn't make sense. So the only solution is $$x=\frac{-5}{6}$$.

DefaultPathway.text: You cannot cancel exponents! $$\frac{a**c}{b**c}\neq$$ $$\frac{a}{b}$$. For example, $$\frac{1^2}{2^2}=\frac{1}{4}$$ is not equal to $$\frac{1}{2}$$.

DefaultPathway.title: Understanding the error
DefaultPathway.text: Numbers in bases cannot move into exponents. $$\frac{a**c}{b**c}\neq a**{c-b},$$ For example, $$\frac14=\frac{1**2}{2**2}\neq 1**{2-2}=1**0=1.$$

DefaultPathway.title: Understanding the error
DefaultPathway.text: $$\frac{\sqrt[n]{a}}{\sqrt[n]{b}}=\sqrt[n]{a}-\sqrt[n]{b}$$ is mixing up laws of exponents and laws of logarithms. For example, consider $$\frac{\sqrt{1}}{\sqrt{4}}=\frac{1}{2},$$ but $$\sqrt{1}-\sqrt{4}=-1.$$

DefaultPathway.title: Understanding the correct choice
DefaultPathway.text: $$\frac{a**c}{b**c}=\left(\frac{a}{b}\right)**c$$ is the law of exponents for quotients with the same exponent and different bases.

title: Exact Values of Trigonometric Functions
body: Find the exact value of the trigonometric function for the given angle in radians.

DefaultPathway.title: Unit Circle Definition
DefaultPathway.text: $$\cos\left(\frac{2\pi}{3}\right)$$ represents the x-coordinate of the point on the unit circle at the angle $$\frac{2\pi}{3}.$$\n##figure1.gif##

DefaultPathway.title: Reference Angle
DefaultPathway.text: The reference angle for $$\frac{2\pi}{3}$$ is $$\frac{\pi}{3}.$$ The absolute values of the coordinates are given by the legs of a $$30-60-90$$ triangle with hypotenuse $$1$$. The x-coordinate length comes from the side adjacent to the 60-degree angle, which is $$\frac{1}{2}.$$\n##figure2.gif##

DefaultPathway.title: Quadrant Sign
DefaultPathway.text: The angle $$\frac{2\pi}{3}$$ is in the second quadrant, where x-coordinates are negative. Therefore, $$\cos\left(\frac{2\pi}{3}\right)=\frac{-1}{2}.$$\n##figure3.gif##

DefaultPathway.title: Unit Circle Definition
DefaultPathway.text: $$\sin\left(\frac{2\pi}{3}\right)$$ represents the y-coordinate of the point on the unit circle at the angle $$\frac{2\pi}{3}.$$\n##figure4.gif##

DefaultPathway.title: Reference Angle
DefaultPathway.text: The reference angle for $$\frac{2\pi}{3}$$ is $$\frac{\pi}{3}.$$ The absolute values of the coordinates are given by the legs of a $$30-60-90$$ triangle with hypotenuse $$1$$. The x-coordinate length is $$\frac{1}{2}.$$ The y-coordinate is obtained from the Pythagorean theorem: $$\sqrt{1**2-\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)**2}=\sqrt{\frac{3}{4}}=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}.$$\n##figure5.gif##

DefaultPathway.title: Quadrant Sign
DefaultPathway.text: The angle $$\frac{2\pi}{3}$$ is in the second quadrant, where $$y-$$ coordinates are positive. Therefore, $$\sin\left(\frac{2\pi}{3}\right)=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}.$$\n##figure6.gif##

DefaultPathway.title: Definition
DefaultPathway.text: $$\tan\left(\frac{2\pi}{3}\right)$$ is the slope of the line connecting the origin to the point on the unit circle at $$\left(\cos\left(\frac{2\pi}{3}\right), \sin\left(\frac{2\pi}{3}\right)\right).$$\n##figure7.gif##

DefaultPathway.title: Coordinate
DefaultPathway.text: The slope is equal to $$\frac{\sin\left(\frac{2\pi}{3}\right)}{\cos\left(\frac{2\pi}{3}\right)}.$$

DefaultPathway.title: Substitute and Divide
DefaultPathway.text: The slope is equal to $$\frac{\sin\left(\frac{2\pi}{3}\right)}{\cos\left(\frac{2\pi}{3}\right)}=\frac{\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}}{-\frac{1}{2}}=-\sqrt{3}.$$

DefaultPathway.title: The correct statement
DefaultPathway.text: The law of logarithms for powers is $$\log_{b}\left(m^n\right)=n\log_{b}\left(m\right)$$. For example, if $$n=3$$, $$\log_{b}\left(mmm\right)=\log_{b}\left(m\right)+\log_{b}\left(m\right)+\log_{b}\left(m\right)=3\log_{b}\left(m\right)$$.

DefaultPathway.text: $$\log_b(1)=\log_b(b**0)=0$$ for any valid base. A base is valid if $$b>0$$ and $$b\neq$$ $$1.$$

DefaultPathway.title: A common error
DefaultPathway.text: A common error is to assume the law of logarithms applies to an expression of the form $$(\log_2(3))**4.$$ It does not! The power must be inside the parentheses! This has no simplified form.

title: You are given that $$\log_b(m)=a$$ and $$\log_b(n)=c.$$
body: The logarithm law for products comes from the exponential law for products with the same base. Explain the reasoning for each step below.

DefaultPathway.title: Definition of the logarithm
DefaultPathway.text: This first step rewrites the given equations using the definition of the logarithm as the inverse of the exponent: $$\log_{b}\left(m\right)=a$$ means $$b^a=m$$, and $$\log_{b}\left(n\right)=c$$ means $$b^c=n$$.

DefaultPathway.title: Law of exponents for products
DefaultPathway.text: This is the law of exponents for products.

DefaultPathway.title: Name the process
DefaultPathway.text: In this step, we take the logarithm of both sides of the equation from step $$2$$.

DefaultPathway.title: What is needed?
DefaultPathway.text: What must be true about $$b$$ to be able to apply the logarithm to both sides of an equation?

DefaultPathway.title: Domain of logarithm
DefaultPathway.text: The logarithm is only defined for positive inputs, which means that we must have $$b>0$$.

DefaultPathway.title: Law of exponents
DefaultPathway.text: We did not apply the law of exponents in this step. We used that in the previous step!

stepAnswer: Cancellation property (logarithm is the inverse of exponentiation)
choices: Cancellation property (logarithm is the inverse of exponentiation)

DefaultPathway.title: Cancellation property
DefaultPathway.text: Logs undo exponents. $$\log_b(b**n)=n$$ for any $$n.$$ In this case, we have $$n=a+c.$$

DefaultPathway.title: Step $$1$$
DefaultPathway.text: Step $$1$$ says $$b^a=m$$ and $$b^c=n$$. Plugging $$m$$ and $$n$$ into the left-hand side of step $$3$$ we get: $$\log_{b}\left(b^a b^c\right)$$ gives $$\log_{b}\left(mn\right)$$.

DefaultPathway.title: Law of logarithms for products
DefaultPathway.text: This is the law of logarithms for products

choices: Apply the law of logarithms for products

DefaultPathway.title: Law of logarithms
DefaultPathway.text: We are actually showing that we get the law of logarithms for products from the law of logarithms for exponents. That is what we are proving. We cannot use the law of logarithms to prove it since that would be circular.

DefaultPathway.title: Substitute the given information into the last step
DefaultPathway.text: This step substitutes the given, $$\log_b(m)=a$$ and $$\log_b(n) $$=$$ $$c, $$ in for $$a$$ and $$c$$ in step $$6$$.

steps.stepTitle: Which of the following is equal to $$\frac{\frac{1}{x}}{\frac{1}{y}}$$? Assume $$x$$ and $$y$$ are both nonzero.

DefaultPathway.title: Definition of division
DefaultPathway.text: Division is the opposite of multiplication.

DefaultPathway.title: Appeal to definition to rewrite
DefaultPathway.text: Dividing by $$\frac{1}{y}$$ is the opposite of multiplying by $$\frac{1}{y}$$. But multiplying by $$y$$ is also the opposite of multiplying by $$\frac{1}{y}$$. Thus dividing by $$\frac{1}{y}$$ is the same as multiplying by $$y!$$

DefaultPathway.title: Full solution
DefaultPathway.text: $$\frac{\frac{1}{x}}{\frac{1}{y}}=\frac{1}{x} y=\frac{y}{x}$$

steps.stepTitle: A student expands $$\left(x-4\right) \left(x+6\right)$$ and gets $$x^2+2x-24$$. Identify the error.
choices: Outer terms added instead of multiplied.

DefaultPathway.title: Factor the expression
DefaultPathway.text: To factor $$x^2+2x-24$$ we want to find numbers $$a$$ and $$b$$ so that $$ab=-24$$ and $$a+b=2$$.

DefaultPathway.title: Conditions on factors
DefaultPathway.text: The sign on the product $$ab=-24$$ tells us that a and $$b$$ have opposite signs. The sign on the sum $$a+b=2$$ tells us that the larger of the two is positive.

DefaultPathway.title: Finding the factors
DefaultPathway.text: The factors of $$24$$ are: $$1$$ and $$24$$, $$2$$ and $$12$$, $$3$$ and $$8$$, and $$4$$ and $$6$$. Notice that the factors $$4$$ and $$6$$ differ by $$2$$. Thus the factorization is $$\left(x-4\right) \left(x+6\right)$$ so that the product is $$-24$$ and the sum is $$2$$.

DefaultPathway.title: FOIL applied
DefaultPathway.text: The first term is $$x^2$$, the outer term is $$-4x$$, the inner term is $$\frac{x}{2}$$, and the last term is $$-2$$ since $$\frac{1}{2}$$ of $$-4$$ is $$-2$$.

DefaultPathway.text: The inner and outer terms combine we have to add $$\frac{1}{2}$$ and $$-4$$, which gives $$\frac{-8}{2}+\frac{1}{2}=\frac{-7}{2}$$.

title: Gear trains and fractions
body: A compound gear train is arranged from left to right. The leftmost driver gear (pink, $$14$$ teeth) meshes with the large gear of a central compound pair (blue, $$42$$ teeth). This blue gear is fixed to the same shaft as a smaller gear (yellow, $$14$$ teeth). The yellow gear meshes with the rightmost driven gear (orange, $$28$$ teeth).\n##figure5.gif

steps.stepTitle: The leftmost gear (pink, $$14$$ teeth) meshes with the larger gear (blue, $$42$$ teeth) of the central compound pair. As the pink gear completes one clockwise rotation, how many times does the blue gear rotate counterclockwise? (Enter your answer as a simplified fraction).
choices: $$\frac{a}{b}=\frac{c}{d}$$ if and only if $$ad=bc$$, and $$b$$ and $$d$$ are nonzero

DefaultPathway.title: How many teeth
DefaultPathway.text: Through the point of connection with the blue gear, the pink gear moves over all $$14$$ teeth through a single rotation.

DefaultPathway.title: How many teeth
DefaultPathway.text: How many teeth of the blue gear pass through the connection point in $$1$$ rotation of the pink gear?

subHints.title: How many teeth
subHints.text: The blue gear is connected to the pink gear. As pink gear rotates once and moves through $$14$$ teeth. The blue gear will also rotate through $$14$$ teeth at the connection point.

DefaultPathway.title: How much did it rotate?
DefaultPathway.text: And $$14$$ teeth out of $$42$$ teeth is $$\frac{14}{42}=\frac{1}{3}$$ of a rotation.

steps.stepTitle: The central compound gear consists of the large blue gear (42 teeth) and a smaller yellow gear (14 teeth) fixed to the same shaft. For every one rotation of the blue gear, how many times does the yellow gear rotate?

DefaultPathway.title: Compound gears are connected
DefaultPathway.text: The yellow gear is connected to the blue gear. They rotate together. So the yellow gear rotates one time for each rotation of the blue gear.

steps.stepTitle: The inner gear of the central compound gear (yellow, $$14$$ teeth) meshes with the rightmost gear (orange, $$28$$ teeth). For every one counterclockwise rotation of the inner central (yellow) gear, how many times does the rightmost (orange) gear rotate?

DefaultPathway.title: Comparing teeth
DefaultPathway.text: The yellow gear has $$14$$ teeth, the orange gear has $$28$$ teeth.

DefaultPathway.title: Comparing rotations
DefaultPathway.text: As the yellow gear rotates once, each of the $$14$$ teeth mesh with the orange gear, rotating it through $$14$$ teeth at the connection point.

DefaultPathway.title: Comparing rotations
DefaultPathway.text: A full rotation of the orange gear uses $$28$$ teeth. Thus rotating through $$14$$ teeth is $$\frac{14}{28}=\frac{1}{2}$$ of a rotation.

steps.stepTitle: A compound gear train is arranged from left to right. The leftmost driver gear (pink, $$14$$ teeth) meshes with the large gear of a central compound pair (blue, $$42$$ teeth). This blue gear is fixed to the same shaft as a smaller gear (yellow, $$14$$ teeth). The yellow gear meshes with the rightmost driven gear (orange, $$28$$ teeth). \n \n Consider the entire gear train described above. If the leftmost (pink) gear rotates at a rate of $$12$$ rotations per minute (RPM), calculate the rotation rate of the rightmost (orange) gear.

DefaultPathway.title: Combining gears
DefaultPathway.text: The rotation rate of each gear combines through a conversion factor problem that connects the rotation rates as products.

DefaultPathway.title: Blue gear rotation rate
DefaultPathway.text: The pink gear rotates at $$\frac{12}{1}$$ RPM. The blue gear rotates at the rate $$\frac{12}{1} \frac{1}{3}=\frac{4}{1}$$ RPM

DefaultPathway.title: Yellow gear rotation rate
DefaultPathway.text: The yellow gear rotates at the same rotation rate as the blue gear, they are connected. The yellow gear rotates at the rate $$\frac{4}{1} \frac{1}{1}$$ RPM.

DefaultPathway.title: Orange gear rotation rate
DefaultPathway.text: The orange gear rotates at the yellow gear's rate times the reduction factor: $$\frac{4}{1} \frac{1}{2}$$ $$=$$ $$2$$ RMP. \n Note that $$\frac{4}{1}$$ is the rotation rate of the yellow gear, and $$\frac{1}{2}$$ is the factor of the number of rotations of the orange gear per rotation of the yellow gear.

title: Defining the logarithm

lesson: A2.1.1 Definitions of Exp and Log

DefaultPathway.title: Base of a logarithm
DefaultPathway.text: Which variable is the base of the logarithm in the equation $$\log_{x}\left(y\right)=z$$?

DefaultPathway.title: Definition connection
DefaultPathway.text: The base is the number that’s repeatedly multiplied to get the argument of the logarithm.

DefaultPathway.title: Log-exponent equivalence
DefaultPathway.text: The equation $$\log_{x}\left(y\right)=z$$ is the same as which exponential equation?

DefaultPathway.title: Connecting logs and exponentials
DefaultPathway.text: $$\log_{x}\left(y\right)=z$$ is saying that $$x^z=y$$. It asks which power of the base gives the argument.

DefaultPathway.title: Eliminate a base
DefaultPathway.text: We can eliminate any choices involving log base $$4$$, because $$4$$ cannot be the base of any equation, since the number $$4$$ raised to an integer power will never be odd. And both $$3$$ and $$81$$ are odd numbers.

DefaultPathway.title: What it means
DefaultPathway.text: Which equation is true?

DefaultPathway.title: Rephrase
DefaultPathway.text: $$\log_{3}\left(81\right)$$ is asking which power of $$3$$ gives $$81$$

DefaultPathway.title: Conclusion
DefaultPathway.text: Rewriting the input in terms of powers of $$3$$ we see that $$\log_{3}\left(81\right)=\log_{3}\left(3^4\right)=4$$.

title: Solve the exponential equation
body: Enter the value of $$x$$

DefaultPathway.title: Write all terms in base $$3$$.
DefaultPathway.text:
$$3**{2x-3}+9**{x-1}=27**{x-2}$$ 
 Notice that the bases and exponents are different. But all bases are powers of $$3$$, so we can write everything in terms of base $$3$$. 

$$3**{2x-3}+(3**2)**{x-1}=(3**3)**{x-2}$$

DefaultPathway.title: Apply the laws of exponentiation for powers
LHS Pull out a factor of $$3**{2x-3}$$
DefaultPathway.text: There is no exponential rule for sums of exponential expressions. To combine the two terms on the left-hand side, we look for a common factor. Observe that $$3**{2(x-1)}=3**{2x-2}=3**{2x-3+1}=3**{2x-3}\cdot $$3.$$

DefaultPathway.title: Carry out the previous step
DefaultPathway.text: Rewrite the left hand side as \n $$3**{2x-3}+3**{2(x-1)}=3**{2x-3}(1+3)$$

DefaultPathway.title: Put it together
DefaultPathway.text: Plugging this into the left-hand side of the equation, we get \n $$3**{2x-3}(1+3)=3**{3(x-2)}$$

DefaultPathway.title: Apply the laws of logarithms
DefaultPathway.text:
Apply the law of logarithms for products to the left-hand side so that 
 $$\log_3(3**{2x-3}(4))=\log_3(3**{3(x-2)})$$ 
 becomes 
 $$\log_3(3**{2x-3})+\log_3(4)=\log_3(3**{3(x-2)})$$

DefaultPathway.title: Apply the cancellation principle
DefaultPathway.text:
Log base $$3$$ undoes exponentiation with base $$3$$. So the equation reduces to 

$$\log_3(3**{2x-3})+\log_3(4)=\log_3(3**{3(x-2)}),$$ which becomes 

$$2x-3+\log_3(4)=3(x-2)$$.

title: Solve the equation involving exponents and logarithms
body: Find $$x$$.

DefaultPathway.title: Apply the law of exponents
DefaultPathway.text: Observe that $$\left(x**3\right)**{\log_x(2)}=\left(x**{\log_x(2)}\right)**3$$

DefaultPathway.title: Simplify using cancellation
DefaultPathway.text: What is $$\left(x**{\log_x(2)}\right)**3$$?

DefaultPathway.title: Plug into original equation
DefaultPathway.text: The original equation has been reduced to $$8\cdot$$ 2**{\log_2(x)}=32$$

DefaultPathway.title: Apply cancellation again
DefaultPathway.text: $$2**{\log_2(x)}=x=4$$ because exponentiation undoes logarithms

title: Solve the equation
body: Find $$x$$.

DefaultPathway.title: Apply cancellation property
DefaultPathway.text: The key here is that logs and exponentiation undo each other, even when the base contains an $$x.$$ Here the base is $$(x+1).$$ \n Just a heads up: at the end, we have to check that $$x+1>0$$ and $$\neq$$ $$1$$ since bases have to be positive and not equal to $$1$$.

DefaultPathway.title: Solve for $$x$$
DefaultPathway.text: $$x^2-1+1=48+1$$ \n $$x^2=49$$ \n The solutions are $$x=\pm 7$$

DefaultPathway.title: Check the domain
DefaultPathway.text: Do both solutions make sense in the original equation?

DefaultPathway.title: Conclusion
DefaultPathway.text: Wait a second, $$\log_{-7+1}=\log_{-6}$$ is not defined. Logarithms must have a positive base, so we must discard the value $$x=-7$$. The only valid solution is $$x=7, $$ which gives a base of $$8$$, and $$8>0$$, $$8\neq$$ $$1, $$ so it works.

title: Solve the exponential equation.
body: Find $$x$$.

DefaultPathway.title: Write in terms of $$y=2^x$$
DefaultPathway.text:
First express each term in terms of $$2^x$$ using laws of exponents. 

$$2**{3x}-2**{x+2}=(2**x)**3-2**x\cdot $$2^2=48$$ 
 Next substitute $$y$$ in for $$2^x$$ everywhere: 

$$(2**x)**3-2**x\cdot $$2^2=y^3-4y=48$$

DefaultPathway.title: Solve for $$y$$
DefaultPathway.text: $$y^3-4y=y\left(y^2-4\right)=\left(y-2\right) y\left(y+2\right)=48$$

DefaultPathway.title: Find a clever solution
DefaultPathway.text: Solving cubics by hand is tricky! In this case, the algebra is telling us we can factor $$48$$ into a product of $$3$$ numbers that differ by $$2$$. That factorization is $$2\cdot$$ $$4$$ $$\cdot$$ $$6=48$$. $$So$$ $$\left(y-2\right) y\left(y+2\right)=2\cdot$$ $$4$$ $$\cdot$$ $$6, $$ so $$y=4$$.

DefaultPathway.title: Don't forget to solve for $$x$$
DefaultPathway.text: Since $$y=4$$, and $$y=2^x$$, we have $$x=2$$.

title: Solve the equation
body: Find $$x$$.

DefaultPathway.title: Apply laws of exponents
DefaultPathway.text: We apply the law of exponents to write everything in base $$2$$. \n $$4**{\log_2(x)}-2**{\log_2(x)}=2**{2\log_2(x)}-2**{\log_2(x)}=12$$

DefaultPathway.title: Apply the laws of logarithms for powers to the first term
Apply cancellation property
DefaultPathway.text: Exponentiation undoes logarithms. This simplifies things!\n$$2**{\log_2(x**2)}-2**{\log_2(x)}=x**2-x=12$$

DefaultPathway.title: Solve for $$x$$ (algebra).
DefaultPathway.text: In the end, it is always algebra. $$x^2-x=12$$ becomes $$x^2-x-12=0$$ which factors as $$\left(x-4\right) \left(x+3\right)=0.$$ The solutions to this equation are $$x=4$$ and $$-3.$$

DefaultPathway.title: Check the domain
DefaultPathway.text: Do both solutions make sense?

DefaultPathway.title: Conclusion
DefaultPathway.text: Only $$x=4$$ makes sense since we cannot input negative values into logarithms.

title: Algebra of fractions
body: Write the given as a single, simplified fraction expression $$\frac{a}{b}$$.

steps.stepTitle: Give $$h\neq$$ $$0, $$ write $$\frac{\frac{1}{x+h}-\frac{1}{x}}{h}=\frac{a}{b}$$ as a single, simplified fraction, cancelling all nonzero terms common to numerator and denominator. \n What is the denominator $$b?$$ (Let all negative signs be carried on the numerator.)

DefaultPathway.title: Find a common denominator
DefaultPathway.text: To perform the operation $$\frac{1}{x+h}-\frac{1}{x}$$, we find a common denominator. That common denominator is the product of the two denominators $$x\left(x+h\right)$$.

DefaultPathway.title: Find a common denominator
DefaultPathway.text: To create an expression with common denominators, we multiply the first term by $$\frac{x}{x}$$ and the second term by $$\frac{x+h}{x+h}$$. \n $$\frac{1}{x+h} \frac{x}{x}-\frac{1}{x} \frac{x+h}{x+h}=\frac{x}{x\left(x+h\right)}-\frac{x+h}{x\left(x+h\right)}$$

DefaultPathway.title: Add numerators
DefaultPathway.text: Apply the rule for adding or subracting fraction with a common denominator: \n $$\frac{a}{c}\pm \frac{b}{c}=\frac{a\pm b}{c}$$.

DefaultPathway.title: Add numerators
DefaultPathway.text: $$\frac{x}{x\left(x+h\right)}-\frac{x+h}{x\left(x+h\right)}=$$ $$\frac{x-(x+h)}{x(x+h)}$$ $$=\frac{\left(-h\right)}{x\left(x+h\right)}$$

DefaultPathway.title: Turn denominator into a fraction
DefaultPathway.text: Write $$\frac{\frac{1}{x+h}-\frac{1}{x}}{h}=\frac{\frac{-h}{x(x+h)}}{h}=\frac{\frac{-h}{x(x+h)}}{\frac{h}{1}}.$$ Here, we used the fact tha $$h=\frac{h}{1}$$.

DefaultPathway.title: Divide fractions
DefaultPathway.text: To divide by a fraction, we multiply by the reciprocal.

DefaultPathway.title: Divide fractions
DefaultPathway.text: $$\frac{\frac{-h}{x(x+h)}}{\frac{h}{1}}=\frac{-h}{x(x+h)}\left(\frac1{h}\right)=\frac{-1}{x(x+h)}$$

steps.stepTitle: What is the numerator $$a$$ when you write $$\frac{\frac{1}{x+h}-\frac{1}{x}}{h}=\frac{a}{b}$$ as a single, simplified fraction $$\frac{a}{b}$$ with common, nonzero terms in numerator and denominator canceled?

DefaultPathway.title: Apply part a
DefaultPathway.text: We saw that $$\frac{\frac{1}{x+h}-\frac{1}{x}}{h}=\frac{-1}{x(x+h)}.$$ The numerator is $$-1$$.

title: Identify the error
body: Select the step that contains the error with algebraic operations.

steps.stepTitle: A student simplified $$\frac{2(x+3)+4}{2}$$ as follows. Identify the step where the error occurred.

DefaultPathway.title: Step $$1$$
DefaultPathway.text: Step $$1$$ applies the distributive property $$a\left(b+c\right)=ab+ac$$. This is carried out correctly. $$2\left(x+3\right)=2x+6$$

DefaultPathway.title: Step $$2$$
DefaultPathway.text: Step $$2$$ combines the constant terms correctly.

DefaultPathway.title: Step $$3$$
DefaultPathway.text: Step $$3$$ incorrectly applies the rule $$\frac{a+b}{c}=\frac{a}{c}+\frac{b}{c}$$. It should be $$\frac{2x+10}{2}=\frac{2x}{2}+\frac{10}{2}$$

DefaultPathway.title: Step $$4$$
DefaultPathway.text: Step $$4$$ correctly cancels the nonzero common factor in numerator and denominator $$\frac{ab}{ac}=\frac{b}{c}$$ and the fact that $$\frac{a}{1}=a$$. This is carried out in the step $$\frac{2x}{2}=\frac{x}{1}=x$$.

title: Identify the equivalent expression
body: Apply algebraic rules for adding fractions and avoid common pitfalls.

steps.stepTitle: Which of the following is equivalent to $$\frac{3}{x-2}+\frac{5}{2-x}?$$

DefaultPathway.title: Observe denominators
DefaultPathway.text: Notice that the denominators are in fact almost equal, but differ by a negative sign. $$2-x=-(x-2)$$

DefaultPathway.title: Pull out negative
DefaultPathway.text: Pull out the negative sign to write as having a common denominator. \n $$\frac{3}{x-2}+\frac{5}{2-x}=\frac{3}{x-2}+\frac{5}{\left(-x-2\right)}$$

DefaultPathway.title: Pull negative from denominator to numerator
DefaultPathway.text: $$\frac{3}{x-2}+\frac{5}{\left(-x-2\right)}=\frac{3}{x-2}+\frac{\left(-5\right)}{x-2}$$

DefaultPathway.title: Add fractions with the same denominator

title: Adding fractions
body: Write as a single fraction and simplify the numerator as much as possible.

steps.stepTitle: Perform the subtraction and simplify the numerator: $$\frac{1}{x+h}-\frac{1}{x}=\frac{A}{x\left(x+h\right)}$$. What is $$A?$$

DefaultPathway.title: Common denominators
DefaultPathway.text: These fractions have unequal denominators. To create equal denominators, multiply the first term by $$\frac{x}{x}$$ and the second term by $$\frac{x+h}{x+h}$$. Remember, multiplying a fraction by $$1$$ doesn't change the term, even if that $$1$$ looks complicated. :)

DefaultPathway.title: Common denominators carried out
DefaultPathway.text: $$\frac{1}{x+h}-\frac{1}{x}=\frac{1}{x+h} \frac{x}{x}-\frac{1}{x} \frac{x+h}{x+h}=\frac{x}{x\left(x+h\right)}-\frac{x+h}{x\left(x+h\right)}$$

DefaultPathway.title: Add fractions with same denominator
DefaultPathway.text: Applying $$\frac{a}{c}-\frac{b}{c}=\frac{a-b}{c}$$ we get \n $$\frac{x}{x\left(x+h\right)}-\frac{x+h}{x\left(x+h\right)}=$$ $$\frac{x-(x+h)}{x(x+h)}$$

DefaultPathway.title: Distribute negative sign
DefaultPathway.text: Don't forget to distribute the negative sign, which is really multiplication by $$(-1)$$ to both terms!

DefaultPathway.title: Distribute negative sign
DefaultPathway.text: $$\frac{x-(x+h)}{x(x+h)}=\frac{x-x-h}{x(x+h)}$$

DefaultPathway.title: Combine like terms
DefaultPathway.text: Recall that $$x-x=0$$, so $$\frac{x-x-h}{x\left(x+h\right)}=\frac{\left(-h\right)}{x\left(x+h\right)}$$

title: Adding fractions
body: Solve for $$x$$ in terms of $$y$$ and $$z$$ given that none are zero.

DefaultPathway.title: Combine terms on the LHS
DefaultPathway.text: $$\frac{1}{z} \frac{y}{y}-\frac{1}{y} \frac{z}{z}=\frac{y}{yz}-\frac{z}{yz}=\frac{y-z}{yz}$$

DefaultPathway.title: Reciprocal trick
DefaultPathway.text: $$\frac{y-z}{yz}=\frac{1}{x}$$ then we can take the reciprocal of both sides, and they will still be equal! Caveat - need to know everything is nonzero, which we are given. Then \n\n$$\frac{yz}{y-z}=\frac{x}{1}=x$$

DefaultPathway.title: Traditional approach
DefaultPathway.text: Find the least common denominator is $$xyz.$$

DefaultPathway.title: Common denominator
DefaultPathway.text: Multiply the entire equation by the least common denominator to eliminate denominators: \n $$\frac{xyz}{z}=\frac{xyz}{x}+\frac{xyz}{y}$$

DefaultPathway.title: Cancel nonzero common factors
DefaultPathway.text: $$xy=yz+xz$$

DefaultPathway.title: Move all $$x$$ terms to LHS
DefaultPathway.text: $$xy-xz=yz$$

DefaultPathway.title: Factor $$x$$
DefaultPathway.text: $$xy-xz=x(y-z)=yz$$

DefaultPathway.title: Isolate $$x$$
DefaultPathway.text: $$x=\frac{yz}{y-z}$$. Note that this forces $$y-z$$ to be nonzero.

steps.stepTitle: Find polynomials P(x) and Q(x) so that the equation below is satisfied. Be sure to note any values of $$x$$ for which this is impossible. $$\frac{P\left(x\right)}{Q\left(x\right)} \frac{3}{x-1}=\frac{x^2}{x-2}-\frac{x+1}{\left(x-2\right)^2}$$

DefaultPathway.title: Can't divide by $$0$$
DefaultPathway.text: $$x$$ cannot equal to which values in this case?

DefaultPathway.title: RHS
DefaultPathway.text: Using the property $$\frac{a}{b}=\frac{a c}{b c}$$, RHS can equal to $$\frac{\left(x-2\right) x^2}{\left(x-2\right)^2}-\frac{x+1}{\left(x-2\right)^2}$$

DefaultPathway.title: RHS
DefaultPathway.text: Using the Distributive Law, $$x^2 \left(x-2\right)=x^3-2x^2$$.

DefaultPathway.title: RHS
DefaultPathway.text: Note $$\frac{a}{b}-\frac{c}{b}=\frac{a-c}{b}$$. Which option is the correct simplification of $$\frac{x^3-2x^2}{\left(x-2\right)^2}-\frac{x+1}{\left(x-2\right)^2}$$?

DefaultPathway.title: $$LHS=RHS$$
DefaultPathway.text: $$\frac{P\left(x\right)}{Q\left(x\right)} \frac{3}{x-1}=\frac{x^3-2x^2-x-1}{\left(x-2\right)^2}$$ since $$LHS=RHS$$.

DefaultPathway.title: $$LHS=RHS$$
DefaultPathway.text: What is $$\frac{P\left(x\right)}{Q\left(x\right)}$$ equal to?

DefaultPathway.title: Simplification
DefaultPathway.text: Using $$\frac{a}{b} \frac{c}{d}=\frac{a c}{b d}$$, which expression is the simplified value of $$\frac{P\left(x\right)}{Q\left(x\right)}$$?

DefaultPathway.title: Conclusion
DefaultPathway.text: We can choose $$P(x)=\left(x^3-2x^2-x-1\right) \left(x-1\right)$$ and $$Q(x)=3\left(x-2\right)^2$$ for $$x \neq 1$$ or $$2$$.

steps.stepTitle: Find all values of $$x$$ satisfying the equation $$\log_{7}(\frac{49(x-1)**3}{x**3-3x-10})=2.$$
steps.stepBody: Hint: Use the laws of logarithms. Remember that for a positive base, one cannot take the logarithm of a negative number.

DefaultPathway.title: Hint
DefaultPathway.text: By the hint, we know $$x-1>0$$, so $$x>1$$, and $$x^3-3x-10>0$$

DefaultPathway.title: LHS
DefaultPathway.text: $$b*(\log_{c}\left(a\right))=\log_{c}\left(a^b\right)$$, so $$\log_{7}\left(49\right)+3*(\log_{7}\left(x-1\right))-\log_{7}\left(x^3-3x-10\right)=\log_{7}\left(49\right)+\log_{7}\left(\left(x-1\right)^3\right)-\log_{7}\left(x^3-3x-10\right)$$

DefaultPathway.title: LHS
DefaultPathway.text: Since $$\log_{c}\left(a b\right)=\log_{c}\left(a\right)+\log_{c}\left(b\right)$$ and $$\log_{c}\left(\frac{a}{b}\right)=\log_{c}\left(a\right)-\log_{c}\left(b\right)$$, so $$\log_{7}\left(49\right)+\log_{7}\left(\left(x-1\right)^3\right)-\log_{7}\left(x^3-3x-10\right)=\log_{7}\left(\frac{49\left(x-1\right)^3}{x^3-3x-10}\right)$$

DefaultPathway.title: $$LHS=RHS$$
DefaultPathway.text: For $$a>0$$, $$\log_{c}\left(a\right)=b$$ implies $$a=c^b$$

DefaultPathway.title: Simplification
DefaultPathway.text: $$\log_{7}\left(\frac{49\left(x-1\right)^3}{x^3-3x-10}\right)=2$$ is equivalent to $$\frac{49\left(x-1\right)^3}{x^3-3x-10}=7^2=49$$

DefaultPathway.title: Simplification
DefaultPathway.text: Divide by $$49$$ on both sides, we get $$\frac{\left(x-1\right)^3}{x^3-3x-10}=1$$

DefaultPathway.title: Simplification
DefaultPathway.text: Since we've showed $$x^3-3x-10>0$$, which one is equivalent to $$\frac{\left(x-1\right)^3}{x^3-3x-10}=1$$?

DefaultPathway.title: Simplification
DefaultPathway.text: Which one is equivalent to $$\left(x-1\right)^3$$?

DefaultPathway.title: Simplification
DefaultPathway.text: Divide by $$3$$ on both sides, we get $$x^2-2x-3=0$$

DefaultPathway.title: Simplification
DefaultPathway.text: $$x^2-2x-3$$ is equivalent to which option?

DefaultPathway.title: Simplification
DefaultPathway.text: $$\left(x-3\right) \left(x+1\right)=0$$, so $$x=3$$ or $$-1$$.

DefaultPathway.title: Simplification
DefaultPathway.text: Since $$x>1$$, what can $$x$$ be?

subHints.title: Double Check
subHints.text: Substitute $$x=3$$ to $$x^3-3x-10$$, we get $$3^3-3\times3-10=8>0$$. So $$x=3$$ is a valid solution.

title: Modeling spread of misinformation exponentially
body: A viral post spreads misinformation online. Initially, $$5$$ people see it. If every hour, each person who has seen it shares it with one new person.
lesson: A2.5.3 Exponents and Logs in the Wild

steps.stepTitle: Write a function for the number of people who have seen the viral post after $$t$$ hours.

DefaultPathway.title: After one hour $$(t=1)$$
DefaultPathway.text: If $$5$$ people see the post initially, $$t=0$$, how many people have seen the post one hour later?

DefaultPathway.title: After two hours $$(t=2)$$
DefaultPathway.text: If $$10$$ people have seen the post after one hour, how many will see the post after $$2$$ hours?

DefaultPathway.title: After $$t$$ hours
DefaultPathway.text: We see that initially, $$5$$ people have seen the post. When $$t=1$$, $$10=5(2)$$ people have seen the viral post. After two hours, $$5(2)(2)=5\left(2^2\right)$$ people have seen the post. To model this exponentially, we see that after $$t$$ hours, $$5\left(2^t\right)$$ people will have seen the post.

steps.stepTitle: How many people have seen the post after $$6$$ hours?

DefaultPathway.title: Plug in the value of time
DefaultPathway.text: Plug in the value of $$t=6$$ into the formula for the number of people who will have seen the post, $$5(2**t).$$

steps.stepTitle: How long (rounded to nearest whole hour) before 10,000 people have seen the misinformation?

DefaultPathway.title: Reframe the question
DefaultPathway.text: The question is asking to find the number of hours $$t$$ such that $$5(2**t)>10,000$$.

DefaultPathway.title: Solve for $$t$$
DefaultPathway.text: Divide both sides by $$5$$ to get 2**t>2,000

DefaultPathway.title: Take the logarithm of both sides
DefaultPathway.text: $$\log_{2}\left(2^t\right)>\log_{2}\left(2, 000\right)$$

DefaultPathway.title: Simplify and compute
DefaultPathway.text: Cancellation on the left gives us $$t>\log_{2}\left(2, 000\right)=10.9$$ hours.

title: Modeling information spread logistically
body:
A town has 10,000 people. A false rumor begins to spread. Initially, $$10$$ people believed it. The spread slows as more people hear of it. After $$3$$ hours, 5,000 people have heard the rumor. 
 
 Assume a logistic model $$N(t)= rac{K}{1+{A10}^{\left(-rtight)}}$$, where 

$$\qquad$$ $$K:$$ total population (maximum number who can hear the rumor), 

$$\qquad$$ $$r:$$ growth rate, 

$$\qquad$$ $$N_0$$: initial number who believe rumor, 

$$\qquad$$ $$A= rac{K-N_0}{N_0}$$.
lesson: A2.5.3 Exponents and Logs in the Wild

steps.stepTitle: Estimate when 9,000 people will have heard the rumor. (Round to the nearest hour.)

DefaultPathway.title: Find the constants
DefaultPathway.text: Determine the constants $$K$$, $$A$$, $$and$$ $$N_0$$ from the problem statement.

DefaultPathway.title: K
DefaultPathway.text: K is the total population of the town, which is 10,000

DefaultPathway.title: $$N_0$$
DefaultPathway.text: $$N_0$$ is the initial number of people who have heard the rumor, which is $$10$$.

DefaultPathway.title: Estimate A
DefaultPathway.text: $$A=\frac{K-N_0}{N_0}=$$ $$\frac{10, 000-10}{10}$$ which is approximately 1,000 since $$10, 000-10$$ is approximately 10,000.

DefaultPathway.title: What are we looking for
DefaultPathway.text: We want to know for which $$t$$ we get $$N(t)=\frac{K}{1+{A10}^{\left(-rt\right)}}=9, 000$$.

DefaultPathway.title: Solve for the growth rate
DefaultPathway.text: Use the fact that after $$3$$ hours 5,000 have heard the rumor to find $$r.$$

DefaultPathway.title: Multiply both sides by the denominator
Apply law of logarithm
DefaultPathway.text: $$-3r=\log_{10}\left(\frac{1}{1000}\right)=\log_{10}\left(1\right)-\log_{10}\left(1000\right)$$

DefaultPathway.title: Solve for $$r$$
DefaultPathway.text: This tells us that \n $$3r=\log_{10}\left(1000\right)=\log_{10}\left({10}^3\right)=3$$, or $$r=1$$.

DefaultPathway.title: Back to the problem
DefaultPathway.text: Now find $$t$$ so that $$N(t)=9, 000$$ given that $$r=1$$.

DefaultPathway.title: Round answer
DefaultPathway.text: To the nearest hour, this is approximately $$4$$ hours before 9,000 people have heard the rumor.

body: You’re trying to guess an $$8$$ letter lowercase password using the English alphabet. No numbers or symbols are used.

steps.stepTitle: How many possible passwords are there?

DefaultPathway.title: Count the passwords
DefaultPathway.text: For an $$8$$ character password with $$26$$ lowercase letters, the total number of possible passwords is has $$26$$ options for $$8$$ placements, which gives $${26}^8$$ possible passwords.

steps.stepTitle: If your program checks $$1$$ million passwords per second, how long would a brute-force algorithm that checks each possible password take? (Enter in hours.)

DefaultPathway.title: Expand the number in scientific notation
Divide by one million
DefaultPathway.text: One million is $${10}^6$$, so checking $$2.1\times{10}^{11}$$ passwords at $${10}^6$$ passwords per second gives $$\frac{2.1\times{10}^{11}}{{10}^6}=2.1\times{10}^5$$ seconds.

DefaultPathway.title: Convert seconds to hours
DefaultPathway.text: There are $$3600={60}^2$$ seconds per hour, so $$\frac{2.1\times{10}^5}{3600}=58$$ hours

steps.stepTitle: If you could reduce the number of possibilities by half at each step (e.g., through clues), how many steps would it take? (Round to the nearest step.)

DefaultPathway.title: Interpret the question
DefaultPathway.text: Recall that a binary search algorithm takes a list of $${26}^8$$ items, and searches them in $$\log_{2}\left({26}^8\right)$$ steps

DefaultPathway.title: Evaluate
DefaultPathway.text: $$\log_{2}\left({26}^8\right)=37.6$$, which is approximately $$38$$ steps

title: Computation time
body: Processing climate data takes $${10}^6\times2^{\left(-\frac{n}{10}\right)}$$ hours with $$n$$ computers.
lesson: A2.5.3 Exponents and Logs in the Wild

steps.stepTitle: How many computers are needed to finish processing climate data in $$24$$ hours? (Round to the nearest computer.)

DefaultPathway.title: Write the equation
DefaultPathway.text: Want to solve $${10}^6\times2^{\left(-\frac{n}{10}\right)}=24$$.

DefaultPathway.title: Isolate $$n$$
DefaultPathway.text: Divide both sides by $${10}^6$$: \n\n$$2^{\left(-\frac{n}{10}\right)}=\frac{24}{{10}^6}$$

DefaultPathway.title: Isolate $$n$$
DefaultPathway.text: To cancel exponentials, apply a logarithm to both sides.

DefaultPathway.title: After applying the logarithm
DefaultPathway.text: Apply log base $$2$$ to both sides of the equation. \n\n$$\log_{2}\left(2^{\left(-\frac{n}{10}\right)}\right)=\log_{2}\left(\frac{24}{{10}^6}\right)$$

DefaultPathway.title: LHS
DefaultPathway.text: Cancel the exponent on the left: \n\n$$\frac{-n}{10}=\log_{2}\left(\frac{24}{{10}^6}\right)$$

DefaultPathway.title: RHS
DefaultPathway.text: Apply law of logarithms for quotients:\n\n$$\frac{-n}{10}=\log_{2}\left(24\right)-\log_{2}\left({10}^6\right)$$

DefaultPathway.title: Eliminate negative signs
DefaultPathway.text: $$\frac{-n}{10}=\log_{2}\left(24\right)-\log_{2}\left({10}^6\right)$$ is the same as $$\frac{n}{10}=\log_{2}\left({10}^6\right)-\log_{2}\left(24\right)$$

DefaultPathway.title: Evaluate
DefaultPathway.text: $$n=10(\log_{2}\left({10}^6\right)-\log_{2}\left(24\right))$$ which is approximately $$153$$ steps

title: Computation accuracy
