DefaultPathway.title: Isolate the exponential
DefaultPathway.text: Divide both sides of the equation by $$85$$.

DefaultPathway.title: Isolate $$n$$
DefaultPathway.text: Logarithms cancel exponents. Apply a logarithm to both sides to bring down the $$n.$$

DefaultPathway.title: Evaluate
DefaultPathway.text: $$n=\log_{1.02}\left(\frac{95}{85}\right)$$ is approximately $$5.6$$

DefaultPathway.title: Interpret result
DefaultPathway.text: To interpret $$5.6$$ as a number of iterations, or discrete steps, we should round up to $$6$$ since after $$5$$ iterations the model will be less than 95% accurate, but by $$6$$ iterations it will be at least 95% accurate.

DefaultPathway.title: Determine the new debt after one month.
DefaultPathway.text:
After one month, you pay 5% of the current debt, which means that your debt decreases: 

$$1000-(0,05)(1000)=1000(1-0.05)=1000(0.95).$$ 

But your debt also increases by 18% of the current debt owed. 

$$\operatorname{1000}\left(0.95ight)+0.18\operatorname{1000}\left(0.95ight)=1000(0.95)(1.18)$$

DefaultPathway.title: Determine the new debt after two months.

steps.stepTitle: How much do you owe after $$3$$ months? (Round to the nearest penny.)

DefaultPathway.title: Units of $$t$$
DefaultPathway.text: The variable $$t$$ is being measured in months.

DefaultPathway.title: Plug in $$t=3$$.
DefaultPathway.text: Plug in $$t=3$$ to find the total credit card debt: $$1000(0.95)**{3}(1.18)**{3}.$$

steps.stepTitle: How much do you owe after $$1$$ year? (Round to the nearest penny.)

DefaultPathway.title: Months in a year
DefaultPathway.text: We need to enter the time of one year in months, which is $$12$$.

DefaultPathway.title: Plug in $$t=12$$.
DefaultPathway.text: Plug in $$t=12$$ to find the total credit card debt: $$1000(0.95)**{12}(1.18)**{12}.$$

DefaultPathway.title: Conclusion
DefaultPathway.text: Observe that in one year, with standard credit card interest rates and payment expectations, the debt is nearly $$4$$ times what it started as! You end up paying more in interest than the original debt in question.

steps.stepTitle: What algebraic rule is used to show that $$(b**a)**c=b**{ac}=b**{ca}=(b**c)**a?$$

DefaultPathway.title: Identify key step
DefaultPathway.text: The key step is that $$b^{ac}=b^{ca}$$.

DefaultPathway.title: Identify the rule
DefaultPathway.text: This step above is true because $$ac=ca$$, which is also known as the commutativity of multiplication.

DefaultPathway.title: Find a counter example
DefaultPathway.text:
To see that a rule is false, we can plug in numbers. For example, let's consider $$x=2$$, $$y=z=1$$, and $$w=0$$. (Keeping numbers small makes it easy!) 
 

Then $${2\left(1+1ight)}^0=2(1)=2$$ but $$\left(2(1)+1(1)ight)**0=1$$.

DefaultPathway.title: Logs undo exponents
DefaultPathway.text:
Logs reverse what an exponential does.

 That means if you take the log base $$2$$ of an exponential with base $$2$$, you get back the power (the exponent).
 $$\log_{2}\left(2^{x+1}ight)=x+1$$

title: Periods of trig functions
body: Which of the following is not a period of the given function.

DefaultPathway.title: Definition of period
DefaultPathway.text: A function is periodic of period $$w$$ if $$p\left(x+kw\right)=p(x)$$ for all $$x, $$ where $$k$$ is a whole number.

DefaultPathway.title: Multiple periods
DefaultPathway.text: $$cos\left(\theta\right)$$ is $$2\pi$$ periodic, because you return to the original position on the circle when you have travelled $$2\pi$$ radians. But you also travel back to the same position after $$4\pi$$ or $$6\pi$$ or $$100\pi$$.

DefaultPathway.title: Not the period
DefaultPathway.text: $$\cos(\theta)$$ is not $$3\pi$$ periodic. For example, $$\cos(0)=1$$ but $$\cos(3\pi)=-1$$.

title: Periods of trig functions
body: Which of the following is not a period of the given function.

DefaultPathway.title: Definition of period
DefaultPathway.text: A function is periodic of period $$w$$ if $$p\left(x+kw\right)=p(x)$$ for all $$x, $$ where $$k$$ is a whole number.

DefaultPathway.title: Multiple periods
DefaultPathway.text: $$sin\left(\theta\right)$$ is $$2\pi$$ periodic, because you return to the original position on the circle when you have travelled $$2\pi$$ radians. But you also travel back to the same position after $$4\pi$$ or $$6\pi$$ or $$100\pi$$.

DefaultPathway.title: Not the period
DefaultPathway.text: $$\sin(\theta)$$ is not $$3\pi$$ periodic. For example, $$\sin(\pi/2)=1$$ but $$\sin(\pi/2+3\pi)=\sin(3\pi/2+2\pi)=-1$$.

title: Periods of trig functions
body: Which of the following is not a period of the given function.

DefaultPathway.title: Definition of period
DefaultPathway.text: A function is periodic of period $$w$$ if $$p\left(x+kw\right)=p(x)$$ for all $$x, $$ where $$k$$ is a whole number.

DefaultPathway.title: Multiple periods
DefaultPathway.text: $$\tan(\theta)$$ is $$2\pi$$ and $$4\pi$$ periodic since it is the ratio of two $$2\pi$$ periodic functions. However, $$\tan(\theta)$$ is also $$\pi$$ periodic. Thus is it $$3\pi$$ periodic as well.

DefaultPathway.title: Not the period
DefaultPathway.text: It is not $$\frac{\pi}{2}$$ periodic. $$\tan(-\pi/4)=-1$$ and $$\tan(-\pi/4+\pi/2)=\tan(\pi/4)=1$$

title: Find the minimal period
body: Find the minimum period of the given function

DefaultPathway.title: The minimum period of $$\cos(\theta)$$
DefaultPathway.text: The minimum period of $$\cos(\theta)$$ is $$2\pi$$

DefaultPathway.title: Relate $$x$$ and $$\theta$$
DefaultPathway.text: To find the period of $$\cos(2\pi$$ $$x), $$ we need to find the range of values for $$x$$ that allows the input to span the same "full circle" as $$\cos(\theta)$$ does for 0< $$\theta$$ <2pi.

DefaultPathway.title: Relate $$x$$ and $$\theta$$
DefaultPathway.text: Set $$2pix=$$ $$\theta$$

DefaultPathway.title: Substitute
DefaultPathway.text: Substitute $$\theta$$ with $$2pix$$ in the standard period interval ( $$0<\theta<2\pi$$ ): \n $$0<2pix<2\pi$$.

DefaultPathway.title: Solve for the interval of $$x$$
DefaultPathway.text: Dividing the entire inequality $$0<2pix<2\pi$$ by $$2\pi$$, we get $$0<x<1$$. Thus, the period is $$1-0=1$$.

title: Find the minimal period

DefaultPathway.title: The minimum period of $$\sin(\theta)$$
DefaultPathway.text: The minimum period of $$\sin(\theta)$$ is $$2\pi$$

DefaultPathway.title: Relate $$x$$ and $$\theta$$
DefaultPathway.text: To find the period of $$\sin(\pi$$ $$x), $$ we need to find the range of values for $$x$$ that allows the input to span the same "full circle" as $$\sin(\theta)$$ does for $$0<\theta<2\pi.$$

DefaultPathway.title: Relate $$x$$ and $$\theta$$
DefaultPathway.text: Set $$pix=$$ $$\theta$$

DefaultPathway.title: Substitute
DefaultPathway.text: Substitute $$\theta$$ with pix in the standard period interval ( $$0<\theta<2\pi$$ ): \n $$0$$ < $$\pi$$ $$x$$ < $$2\pi$$.

DefaultPathway.title: Solve for the interval of $$x$$
DefaultPathway.text: Dividing the entire inequality $$0$$ < $$\pi$$ $$x$$ < $$2\pi$$ by $$\pi, $$ we get $$0<x<2$$. Thus, the period is $$2-0=2$$.

title: Find the minimal period
body: Find the minimum period of the given function

DefaultPathway.title: The minimum period of $$\tan(\theta)$$
DefaultPathway.text: The minimum period of $$\tan(\theta)$$ is $$\pi$$

DefaultPathway.title: Relate $$x$$ and $$\theta$$
DefaultPathway.text: To find the period of $$\tan\left(\frac{\pi}{4}x\right), $$ we need to find the range of values for $$x$$ that allows the input to span the same range as $$\tan(\theta)$$ does for $$0<\theta<\pi.$$

DefaultPathway.title: Relate $$x$$ and $$\theta$$
DefaultPathway.text: Set $$\frac{pix}{4}=$$ $$\theta$$

DefaultPathway.title: Substitute
DefaultPathway.text: Substitute $$\theta$$ with $$\frac{pix}{4}$$ in the standard period interval ( $$0<\theta<2\pi$$ ): \n $$0<\frac{pix}{4}<\pi$$.

DefaultPathway.title: Solve for the interval of $$x$$
DefaultPathway.text: Dividing the entire inequality 0< $$\frac{\pi$$ $$x}{4}$$ < $$\pi$$ by $$\frac{\pi}{4}$$, we get $$0<x<\operatorname{\pi}\left(\frac{4}{\pi}\right)=4$$. Thus, the period is $$4$$.

title: Relating period and frequency
body: Choose the options that best finishes the statement provided.

DefaultPathway.title: Period
DefaultPathway.text: The function $$\cos(wx)$$ traverses its full range $$0<wx<2\pi$$, which is equivalent to $$0<x<\frac{2\pi}{w}$$

DefaultPathway.title: Period
DefaultPathway.text: The period is $$\frac{2\pi}{w}$$

DefaultPathway.title: Reciprocal relationship
DefaultPathway.text: The relationship for the period $$\frac{2\pi}{w}$$ is inverse in w. As w increases, the period decreases. (Similarly, as $$w$$ decreases, the period increases.)

steps.stepTitle: Which of the following is equivalent to the expression $$\frac{\sin(2x)}{1+\cos(2x)}?$$

DefaultPathway.text: $$2\cos**2(\theta/2)=1+\cos(\theta)$$ \n Now we have rearranged the half angle formula to match the structure that we see in our problem.
